messages.author: 7f87f78f0cd24437
messages.subject: Distance in R - comparison of pooled CDS, stratified CDS and MCDS
parts:
Hello Everyone,

 

I am working with some bird point count data collected in binned distances. There are a total of 12 sites, 3 in each of 4 forest age classes. I would like to find out if there are differences in detectability between the age classes. I am using the package ‘Distance’ in R.

 

I have some queries and concerns, and would really appreciate some guidance:

 

Q1. I have attempted to use the “gof_ds” call to test for model fit. However, there are generally only two outcomes. Sometimes I get p-values of 0, does this suggest that fits are very poor? Alternatively, I get “No degrees of freedom for test”, presumably because there are a lot of parameters in my models. Is it still legitimate to continue with the distance sampling process if I can’t test for model fit? (I think that it means that I can’t know if the AIC selection is choosing a model with poorer fit, is that right?)

 

Q2. I have been following the approach of the Marques et al. (2007) Amakihi paper, i.e. I have conducted pooled CDS, stratified CDS, and MCDS. In Table 2 (p.1239) of their paper, Marques et al. present a combined summary of the model selection. How are they able to report a single combined model selection for the stratified analyses, when they have stratified their data by 7 time periods? I have done this for the 4 forest age classes, and so I have four sets of model selections, with different models selected for each age class. How could I combine these into a single selection procedure? (And would that even make sense, given that different models are selected for different age classes?)

 

Q3. In addition, in Table 2, Marques et al. compare all of the models for both pooled and stratified analyses, when presumably the models are based on different data (i.e. the full dataset for pooled CDS and MCDS, but only subsets for the stratified CDS). Is that correct? And if so, does this not matter? I think that I must have misunderstood their approach, but I don’t know which aspects I am failing to get my head around.

 

Q4. Leaving aside the issue with the stratified analyses, I have tried model selection with just the pooled CDS and the MCDS with forest age as a covariate. (I have also tried individual sites as well, but I haven't combined forest age and site because I assume that they will be correlated). In Marques et al., the MCDS models have lower AICs than the pooled CDS models, so the former are preferred. However, it is the opposite in my model selection process. The pooled CDS is chosen over the MCDS (see table below). Does this mean that the forest age covariate is not improving model fit? And therefore I can conclude that there are similar levels of detectability between forest age classes? Although I also note that the preferred models have a lot of adjustments in them, and that the model with Forest.Age as a covariate is simpler. Perhaps arguing the reverse, that forest age is influencing detectability.

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Distance in R - comparison of pooled CDS, stratified CDS and MCDS
parts:
Tom

You ask a series of good questions.  I'll not try to answer all of them, but make a few comments:

Q1 - your are correct in your interpretations; by binning data at time of data collection, you limit the types of analyses you can conduct.  Degrees of freedom available for a chi-square goodness of fit test is (number of distance bins) - 1 - (parameters in model).  You are left with assessment of fit based upon visual assessment of the fitted pdf to the histogram.  You can at least say something about the agreement between your data and the fitted values.

Q2 - I haven't looked at this for a while so I don't know the details of the stratified analysis of Marques et al. (2007).  Fortunately, if you have downloaded the GUI version of Distance (as opposed to the R package), you have the analyses performed by Marques et al. (2007) in a project called "Amakihi.dst"--you can pour over the details yourself.

Q3 - see Q2

Q4 - Recognise the covariates used in Marques et al. (2007) were observer and minutes after sunrise.  Both have fairly obvious relationships to detectability; it is less obvious that forest age or site might be influential in detectability; but it is difficult to speak in generalities about your particular study.  One comment I would mention regarding the results you provide is the really small P_a estimates of nearly all of your models.  The estimates you show suggest the detection function is falling away very rapidly and that for each bird you detect in your plots, there are 10 more you don't detect.  That's going to make for a difficult inference task.

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Distance in R - comparison of pooled CDS, stratified CDS and MCDS
parts:
Hello Eric,

Many thanks for your responses, particularly in terms of Q1, and how to proceed when unable to conduct a goodness-of-fit test.

In reference to Q's 2 & 3, I contacted Tiago Marques about this. He very kindly offered some advice, which I will share here in case anyone here has a similar situation. The program Distance (as opposed to Distance for R) automatically calculates a total AIC value for stratified analyses (i.e. a single value across all strata). To obtain equivalent values when using the R package, one can sum the AIC for each stratum-specific model with the AIC values for the corresponding models in the other strata. This combined value can then be compared with the pooled analyses in AIC model selection.

In regards to Q4, I absolutely agree Eric, there isn't a huge reason to expect habitat age will affect detectability, but for my study it is important to be able to discount that possibility.

Thanks again,
Tom
